sentences.text: Nundasuchus is an extinct genus of crurotarsan archosaurs, a group likely related to Paracrocodylomorpha.
Unlike modern crocodilians, this animal stood with its legs positioned directly underneath its body.
Its palate featured unusual pterygoid teeth along the midline, a feature rare among archosaurs.
The neural spines expanded into heart-shaped structures at their upper front tips, similar to those found in Batrachotomus.
Most back vertebrae were tall, concave on both ends, and possessed a pair of ventral keels separated by a shallow groove.
The second sacral rib was flatter and tilted diagonally so that its rear edge stood higher than its front edge.
The scapula was paddle-like and relatively small in size.
The lower edge of this scapula connected to a semicircular coracoid bone.
A wide groove appeared below the glenoid of the scapula, a feature similar to that found in aetosaurs and Postosuchus.
The pubis bone is characteristically small, measuring only about 30% of the femur's length.
The femur is S-shaped, with the femoral head twisted inwards and the distal condyles twisted outwards.
This twist creates a 45-degree angle between the extremities, a trait shared with most eucrocopodans except dinosaurs.
The lateral side of the calcaneal tuber has a noticeable pad that appears unique to this species.
The upper surface of the calcaneum connects to the fibula via a convex, barrel-shaped joint.
The front edge of the astragalus has a large concave surface called an astragalar hollow overlying a small convexity called an astragalar ball.
The ventral keels are considered a unique trait among archosaurs and likely evolved convergently with similar structures in the unrelated aquatic archosauriform Vancleavea.
A noticeable pad on the lateral side of the calcaneal tuber appears unique to this species.
The genus is known only from the holotype specimen NMT RB48, a partially complete and disarticulated skeleton housed at the National Museum of Tanzania.
Nundasuchus was first described and named by Sterling J. Nesbitt, Christian A. Sidor, Kenneth D. Angielczyk, Roger M. H. Smith, and Linda A. Tsuji in 2014.
Fossils come from the Manda Beds of the Middle Triassic in southwest Tanzania.
Only one species, Nundasuchus songeaensis, is known from a single partial skeleton containing vertebrae, limb elements, osteoderms, and skull fragments.
Members of this genus were likely carnivores with ziphodont, steak-knife-like teeth and rows of bony plates called osteoderms along their backs.
Many studies consider Nundasuchus a pseudosuchian, meaning it was more closely related to modern crocodilians than to dinosaurs.
Nesbitt (2011) considered crocodylomorphs to be descended from taxa traditionally identified as "rauisuchians".
One hypothesis, supported by its 2014 description, considers Nundasuchus to be more "advanced" than basal groups rather than closer to Ticinosuchus and paracrocodylomorphs.

Some phylogenetic analyses place Nundasuchus at the base of the group, sometimes with phytosaurs, based on plesiomorphic traits such as palatal teeth, a short pubis, and certain calcaneal characteristics.
Nundasuchus lived in what is now Tanzania, Africa, approximately 240 million years ago.
Based on comparisons with South African fauna, the fossil beds are dated to the Anisian stage of the early Middle Triassic.
Scientists debate the exact classification of Nundasuchus relative to other pseudosuchians.
Some researchers suggest Nundasuchus belongs near the base of the pseudosuchian group alongside phytosaurs, citing primitive features like palate teeth and a short pubis.
Another hypothesis posits that Nundasuchus is more advanced and closer to Ticinosuchus and paracrocodylomorphs, a view supported by its 2014 description.
The original description of Nundasuchus vertebrae suggested the possible presence of hyposphene-hypantrum articulations.
A 2018 study disputed the presence of hyposphene-hypantrum articulations in Nundasuchus, arguing they were misidentified parts of the zygapophyses.
It is debated whether Nundasuchus is a basal pseudosuchian with convergent traits or an archosauriform closely related to Archosauria with convergent features.
